extracted.intended_audience: professional scientists and informed readers of Nature (primarily physicists and chemists)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying criteria used in the article to judge scientific hypotheses, experimental reports, and historical-archaeological arguments in physics and chemistry conference reporting. Emphasis is on what makes a satisfactory explanation, experimental result, or interpretive inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use statistical/distributional evidence to infer calendar systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Infer the structure of an underlying calendar or ritual year from counts and distributions of fairs (e.g., totals of fairs in February, May, August, November; combinations of quarter days; astronomical vs. church dates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author tabulates fairs by date and county, compares totals (e.g., '1425' vs. '1571' estimates), examines combinations of quarter days, and uses prevalence ratios (February:May:August:November ≈ 1:3:2:2) to argue for the primacy of the May-year. Include nearby shifted dates (±11 days) and two-day fairs as evidence of originally contiguous festival periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlate archaeological/astronomical alignments with local traditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Strengthen hypotheses about ancient festival sites by showing parallelism between archaeological alignments (e.g., Stonehenge avenues), astronomical dates, and the prominence of local fairs and traditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article argues that astronomical, historical, and ferial evidence together point to Stonehenge as a May temple — use multiple independent lines of evidence (alignments, literary sources like Geoffrey of Monmouth, place-fair dates, inscriptions) for a convincing case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use epigraphic and material finds as corroboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ inscriptions and archaeological finds (e.g., dedications equating Celtic gods with Roman ones) to support interpretive claims about local ritual or cultural practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: Roman inscriptions to Celtic Neptune or Maponos near Lydney and Hexham are used to buttress links between sites and ritual/temple functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for calendar drift and shifted festival observance
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and incorporate shifts in observed dates (e.g., ±11 days) due to calendar changes or local practice when matching modern fair dates to older quarter days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author includes fairs observed on dates such as April 23/May 4 or April 26/May 6 and explicitly claims older dates where two-day fairs connect adjacent days; treat these shifted dates as part of the same festival series rather than as independent anomalies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory completeness for physical theories (aurora example)
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfactory physical theory must explain the full range of observed phenomena (e.g., geographic localization near magnetic poles, timing of auroral displays, 'dark segment', intensifications, 'dancing' rays), not just reproduce some experimental analogues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commentary on Villard notes that while laboratory magnet+kathode-ray experiments produce aurora-like phenomena, 'Those actually familiar with auroral phenomena will think of a number of points requiring explanation to which M. Villard does not refer.' A robust theory must address timing (evening vs morning predominance), structure (bright patches and dark segments), dynamics (apparent motion), and relationship to magnetic disturbances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source and mechanism specification for proposed agents
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorists must state plausible sources and mechanisms for the agents invoked (e.g., whether electrified particles originate from the Sun, cirrus clouds, or cosmic dust) and explain how those sources produce the observed effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Villard is critiqued for not dogmatising the origin of ions; Arrhenius postulates a solar origin taking ~2 days, while Villard favours ions starting in the atmosphere (e.g., negatively charged ice particles in cirrus). The origin affects predictions (timing, charge sign) and thus is essential to evaluate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make testable, charge-dependent predictions
rubrics_metrics.description: A physical theory should make concrete, testable predictions (e.g., sign of particle charge implies evening vs morning aurora) that can be used to confirm or falsify it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Villard's scheme requires that the particles be negatively charged to match the observed evening aurora; if positive, the aurora would be expected in the early morning. Such specific predictions are valuable for assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate laboratory analogues and connect to observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use laboratory experiments (e.g., magnetised sphere + cathode rays) to reproduce phenomena analogous to nature and then relate the lab configurations to geophysical conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prof. Birkeland's and Villard's magnet experiments are cited as producing aurora-like effects; authors should explain which experimental features correspond to observed phenomena (e.g., bright patches as superposition of direct and return paths).

rubrics_metrics.name: Test structural/crystallographic hypotheses against all physical properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed crystal-structure hypotheses (e.g., closest packing of 'spheres of influence') must be tested not only by geometric form (axial ratios) but by all relevant physical properties (cleavage, twinning, gliding, thermal behaviour, sudden volume changes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prof. Sollas objected that the suggested structure for silver iodide did not explain sudden thermal volume contraction. Prof. Miers emphasised that 'this principle must be tested by all the physical properties as well as the geometric form of the crystals.' Use models and experimental data to validate structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use models, demonstrations and quantitative indices
rubrics_metrics.description: Support theoretical proposals with physical models, quantitative indices (e.g., axial ratios as an index of packing closeness), and detailed calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speakers showed models to illustrate alternative systems; Dr. Tutton suggested using topic axial ratios as a measure of packing closeness. Where possible, construct and display models and compute theoretical ratios for comparison with observed crystals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain connection between science and practical/industrial concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific work and training should preserve strong links with manipulative skill and industry-relevant problems; applied relevance is an evaluative virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The president's address warned against neglecting manipulative skill in young chemists and the meeting valued discussions (e.g., strength/quality of flour) that connect science and industry. Preference is given to work that clarifies contentious practical questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide clear experimental/technical procedure and practical guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting experimental methods (e.g., preparation of reagents like Grignard reagents), provide clear, detailed, and practically valuable procedural information for future workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dr. Alex McKenzie's detailed account of the preparation of the Grignard agent is praised as 'of the utmost value to future workers.' Reports should include preparation details, conditions, and cautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive utility for engineering applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Research and measurements should yield predictive rules or parameters that inform engineering design (e.g., predicting ignition temperatures of gas mixtures to choose compression spaces in engines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mr. Dugald Clerk emphasised the importance of being able to predict ignition temperature from mixture composition to avoid pre-ignition in large gas engines; applied predictive ability is a criterion of usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report and interpret anomalous or distinguishing experimental signatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and explain distinctive experimental signatures (e.g., absorption bands, conductivity maxima, unusual stability toward reagents) that characterise new compounds or materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports such as iron tetracarbonyl showing a 'characteristic absorption band in the yellow' or pyridonium salts showing 'abnormally high conductivity' illustrate that clear spectroscopic/conductivity signatures should be measured and interpreted when introducing new substances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge limitations and avoid dogmatism where mechanism uncertain
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should acknowledge theoretical uncertainties and avoid overclaiming when mechanisms remain speculative or incompletely established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Villard 'is not prepared to dogmatise' about how ions get into motion; the report notes that some proposals 'seem still in a somewhat uncrystallised state.' Explicitly flagging limitations helps readers weigh claims appropriately.
